channels.name: ads on tiktok, facebook, and pinterest
channels.note: Performance ads with a wow promise drive this niche: new hairstyles, photos coming to life, glossy avatars. More than half the mentions are angry because the result didn't match the video. The channel works, but the promise in the ad has to match the product, otherwise you get a flood of one-star reviews.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: People google and search the store with a specific job in mind: a free editor, a talking avatar. Search ranking makes the call, one person flat out says they trusted the high rating in Google search.

channels.name: word of mouth and buzz
channels.note: Some people install the app simply because everyone around them is talking about it. The signal is weak and fuzzy, nothing to build on, but it shows that viral waves do happen in this niche.

channels.name: reddit recommendations
channels.note: A single but telling signal: for professional headshots people go to reddit for advice, not to ads. If the product actually delivers a business-grade portrait, a reddit thread brings in motivated paying users.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The main entrance to the niche. People come with a very specific pain: organizing a novel, writing for free, generating poems, helping a student with an essay. Whoever closes the narrow query first in store search takes the install.

channels.name: switching from another tool
channels.note: The second door: users leave Grammarly, ChatGPT, and dead services like Google Inbox. Disappointment in the leader creates a ready-made capture moment, and positioning as an alternative to X without its pain works.

channels.name: ads on tiktok and instagram
channels.note: Social ads bring people in, but both mentions in reviews are angry: the app doesn't do what the video showed. The channel is there, trust in it within the niche is not.

channels.name: school requirement
channels.note: A single signal: a school hands out a subscription, the student gets used to the tool and brings it home. For writing and note-taking apps, education licenses work as a quiet recruitment channel.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends and acquaintances
channels.note: Astrology gets passed from hand to hand: a friend showed it, a girlfriend suggested checking compatibility. A product with shared charts and couple comparison naturally nudges people to invite their own, Co-Star and The Pattern have it built into the mechanics.

channels.name: influencers and tiktok
channels.note: Spiritual bloggers on TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram push specific apps at scale, and people install them on direct tips. But the channel is already burnt: half the reviews accuse influencers of being paid shills and the app of botched calculations.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: Part of the audience searches deliberately: tracking moon cycles, learning astrology, replacing an app they got tired of. The queries are narrow, and the learning niche looks underserved, one person complains outright that there's nothing here to learn astrology from.

channels.name: ads on youtube and facebook
channels.note: The aggressive ad buying in this niche comes from fortune-telling services like Kasamba, and both complaints seethe with irritation: the ads stalk people and prey on emotions. For an honest product this is more of a cautionary tale than a channel.

channels.name: mom-to-mom word of mouth: friends and family
channels.note: The liveliest channel in the niche. A new mom gets the app from another mom, a sister, or a sister-in-law, often in the very first weeks after birth. A product that genuinely saves you in the newborn fog gets recommended onward all by itself.

channels.name: switching from another tracker
channels.note: Parents easily ditch a tracker that broke, drowned in ads, or lost data, and install the next one right away. A separate mechanic: pregnant users graduate from a pregnancy app into the same brand's baby tracker, Philips runs this funnel out in the open.

channels.name: advice from doctors and consultants
channels.note: Pediatricians, therapists, and lactation consultants hand out apps like prescriptions, one consultant writes outright that she recommends the tracker to moms in the NICU. Getting into these specialists' toolkits means users arriving in batches.

channels.name: podcasts
channels.note: Indie tracker Mango Baby was found through podcasts both times, once via a mention by a tech show host. For a small product with no budget, landing in a podcast that expecting parents listen to converts straight into paying users.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The dominant channel in the niche. People spend years cycling through planners chasing one specific wish: tasks and calendar in a single widget, a circular day dial, a simple list with no bloat. The winner is whoever nails the niche request exactly, not whoever has the most features.

channels.name: switching from another planner
channels.note: A niche classic: leaving Todoist over price, Wunderlist after it shut down, Google Calendar for a shared calendar for two. A competitor's death or greed delivers already-trained users ready to pay less for the same thing.

channels.name: word of mouth: family and friends
channels.note: A planner spreads through the inner circle: a husband talks his wife into it, a friend glances at someone's screen and buys it for herself. Shared calendars and lists turn every user into a recruiter, they personally need their people inside.

channels.name: work requirement
channels.note: A single signal, but it's there: an employer imposes a shared team calendar and the person lives in the app whether they like it or not. The channel brings users without love, but in bulk and for the long haul.

channels.name: switching from another exchange or a bank
channels.note: The biggest visible channel: people deliberately look for a Coinbase alternative, flee an exchange after bad support, or move money out of a regular bank for the investing features. A new product wins by planting itself squarely on a specific giant's pain point.

channels.name: word of mouth: investor friends
channels.note: People get walked into crypto by the hand: a friend who's already in sets the newbie up with a specific app. Trust is worth more than advertising here, because money and the fear of getting scammed are on the line.

channels.name: podcasts and crypto media
channels.note: Bitcoin podcasts and shows like Banter Bubbles bring users directly, one person admits they never would have heard of the exchange otherwise. Niche media solves the trust problem better than banner ads.

channels.name: crypto conferences
channels.note: A single but curious signal: a user got recruited at a Consensus conference booth, then went and googled whether it was a scam. Offline events build awareness, but the reputation check still happens no matter what.

channels.name: word of mouth and someone else's success
channels.note: Explicit signals in this niche are surprisingly rare: the giants live on brand recognition, which nobody writes about in reviews. What's left is this: a friend recommended it, or someone watched the app work for an acquaintance and went to try it themselves.

channels.name: therapist's advice
channels.note: Therapists nudge clients to get back out there after breakups, and a dating app becomes the first step. The channel isn't about a specific brand, it's about the moment of entering the niche, which you can catch with fresh-start content.

channels.name: searching for free apps
channels.note: Some people just google free dating apps and install whatever has a decent rating. The promise of free drives the install, and the betrayed expectation of hidden payments breeds angry reviews.

channels.name: youtube ads
channels.note: The only explicit ad mention, and a hostile one at that: the person saw Tinder's videos on YouTube but never finished signing up. Mass ad buying delivers reach but doesn't remove the distrust at the door.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The main entrance: people search for a fix to a specific pain, focus music, doomscroll blocking, an exam timer. It's often a long slog of I've tried everything, so the winner is the app that worked where the others wore out their welcome.

channels.name: social media posts and ads
channels.note: The irony of the niche: people find doomscroll blockers while doomscrolling. A Pinterest post about studying, a find in the Instagram feed, a Facebook ad. The audience literally lives in the very place it wants to escape, and that's the best targeting for anti-scroll products.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends and family
channels.note: People with ADHD and phone addiction share what finally worked, and that kind of advice outweighs any ad. A sweet detail: a son brought his dad the game app from Hank Green, and now the whole family plays.

channels.name: a familiar offline brand
channels.note: A single but telling signal: a teacher uses physical Time Timer timers in class and installed their app because of it. A recognizable offline object pulls installs without any store marketing.

channels.name: word of mouth: referral links and gift cards
channels.note: The only explicit trace in the reviews: people get brought into food delivery by someone close, via a referral link or a gift card. There's no organic saw it on social media or doctor recommended it here, the niche runs on brand and promos, so a new app should build referral mechanics in from day one.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The dominant channel: people head to the store for a habit tracker on their own and methodically try apps until one fits. Reviews openly mention dozens of attempts, which means a new app genuinely makes the shortlist if the screenshots instantly show simplicity and an honest freemium.

channels.name: social media ads
channels.note: The niche leaders buy ads on Facebook, Instagram, and Reddit, but in reviews this channel mostly surfaces with anger: the promise in the video doesn't match the product. The channel drives installs, and the betrayed expectations then hit the rating.

channels.name: ai chat suggestion
channels.note: A fresh channel: someone asks ChatGPT what to track routines with, gets a couple of names, then checks them against store reviews. Just one signal so far, but it shows that landing in AI answers already brings installs.

channels.name: therapist recommendation
channels.note: Trackers with a self-care bent get recommended by therapists as a simple tool for clients with low motivation. One explicit signal, but it comes from the practitioner's side, meaning the channel scales through practitioners, not patients.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The main channel: people spend years cycling through journals and mood trackers with a very specific ask, custom prompts, photos attached to entries, cross-platform sync, a passcode lock. A new app just needs to name one such scenario precisely in its title and screenshots to enter that rotation.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends and loved ones
channels.note: A journal is an intimate thing, and a personal recommendation is what lowers the trust barrier: a friend showed it, a buddy suggested it. People write outright that they couldn't start journaling until someone close brought them the app.

channels.name: therapist's orders
channels.note: Therapists assign mood trackers as homework for working through emotions, and those users arrive already motivated. For a new app this is a channel through practitioners' offices, not through ads.

channels.name: YouTube and Instagram content
channels.note: Isolated but lively signals: people find the app through a YouTube video or an Instagram recommendation. Cute customizable journals show beautifully on video, it's a natural format for promoting them.

channels.name: app store search for the language
channels.note: People search for an app for a specific language or format, Levantine Arabic, sign language, stories instead of flashcards, and check the rating before paying. A rare language or a rare format brings installs on its own, the giants leave those shelves empty.

channels.name: ads and reels on social media
channels.note: TikTok, Instagram reels, and Facebook ads bring people in steadily, and showing the actual mechanic works best, like Teuida's storytelling. The flip side: if the video promises something the product doesn't have, the review comes back scorched.

channels.name: fleeing Duolingo
channels.note: A noticeable stream of installs comes from people Duolingo angered with hearts, weak courses for rare languages, or bugs, and they hunt for a replacement on purpose. A new app wins by answering the Duolingo replacement query head-on in its positioning.

channels.name: free access through the library
channels.note: Public libraries in the US give away subscriptions to language apps for free, and people arrive through that exact door. For a new product it's a ready-made B2B2C channel: a deal with library networks brings loyal users at zero acquisition cost.

channels.name: doctor's and therapist's orders
channels.note: The most powerful channel in the niche: apps get recommended by therapists, doctors, psychologists, and even nurses, both to patients in the office and in their own name in reviews. The user arrives with trust already in place, so for a new app this is a channel through practitioners, not through the stores.

channels.name: the founder's media footprint
channels.note: People are drawn by the teacher's persona: Andy Puddicombe through a Netflix series, Sam Harris through podcasts and books, Mindvalley through its own YouTube. In meditation people subscribe to a voice and an authority, so the founder's personal media content works as a funnel.

channels.name: insurance and employer
channels.note: A noticeable share of users gets the subscription free through an employer or health insurance, up to and including a direct recommendation from the insurer. For a new app this points to corporate wellness programs as a distribution channel.

channels.name: Instagram and Facebook ads
channels.note: Giants like Calm flood Instagram and Facebook with ads promising a personal plan, and it does drive subscriptions. But in reviews the channel mostly shows up through disappointment: the promised content isn't in the catalog and the person feels cheated.

channels.name: the network pulls: friends and family are already there
channels.note: The messenger classic: people install the app not because they like it but because their people are in it. In reviews it's literal, I'm only here because I got dragged in. A new messenger needs a scenario where one user brings their whole group at once.

channels.name: work or school requirement
channels.note: The second strongest channel: an employer or school picks the messenger for you, and you're stuck using it even if you hate it. For a B2B messenger this means selling to the administration, not the user, but retention is guaranteed.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: Works in the utilitarian sub-niches: a second number, spam blocking, bulk messaging. The person shows up with a specific pain, tries options from the store, and stays with the first one that actually works.

channels.name: youtubers and streamers
channels.note: Entertainment video chats get discovered through youtubers' videos: a creator plays with random strangers, viewers go to recreate it. A narrow channel, but for apps with a spectacle-worthy mechanic it's a ready-made content format.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: People arrive with a specific scenario the giants don't cover: a player for music on Google Drive or OneDrive, background playback for niche tracks, simple radio. They comb the store until something works and gladly pay for a bullseye.

channels.name: fleeing Spotify and YouTube Premium
channels.note: A steady stream of installs: prices and policies of the big platforms squeeze people out, and they go looking for an escape hatch on purpose. A new player wins by saying Spotify replacement without a subscription out loud and making playlist import the first screen.

channels.name: moving from a dead player
channels.note: Small players die regularly, vanish from the store, or break, and their audience goes house-hunting in an organized way. Whoever catches the exodus wave first collects trained users with formed habits for free.

channels.name: word of mouth: family and social media
channels.note: Rare but explicit signals: the app comes from someone close or from a stranger's tip on social media. In music, a personal recommendation competes with the force of habit, so the channel is weaker than in other niches.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: People spend years hunting for a notes app that matches an exact ask: a sticky-notes replacement, saved messages like in Telegram, full-text search with highlighting, working without an account. The queries are hyper-specific, and an app that honestly closes one of them gets found on its own.

channels.name: moving from Evernote and the other giants
channels.note: A steady refugee stream: Evernote with its pricing, OneNote with its lag, the dead Outlook Notes. People arrive with years of archives and pay right away if there's easy import. Exodus waves from the giants remain the main audience-capture moment in the niche.

channels.name: recommendations on Reddit and from coworkers
channels.note: PKM tools get recommended in professional circles: a Reddit thread on what to use instead of Evernote, or a coworker at the office. The recommendation arrives bundled with a work scenario, so these users take root in the product fast.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: People walk into the store with the phrase already formed: calorie tracker, menu planner, fasting timer. They pick by search suggestions, rating, and the first reviews, so a name that matches the query plus early ratings decide everything.

channels.name: TikTok and Instagram ads
channels.note: People readily try diet ads from the feed, but they get angry when the store price doesn't match the promise in the video. The channel works, and trust burns down at the first mismatch.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends
channels.note: People start counting calories for company: a friend recommends what worked for them. Those who come via recommendation head straight for the feature they were invited for.

channels.name: doctor's orders
channels.note: Doctors and dietitians send patients off to keep a food diary. The signals are few, but these are the most motivated users, with a medical task and strict tracking requirements.

channels.name: word of mouth: girlfriends and family
channels.note: A cycle tracker gets passed from hand to hand: a friend, a sister, a girlfriend. The topic is intimate, so a personal recommendation outweighs the rating. A new app needs something worth retelling, accuracy or a partner mode.

channels.name: Facebook and TikTok ads
channels.note: Targeting a specific symptom and positioning both work: Flo catches menopause through Facebook ads, Clue gets pushed on TikTok as made by women. The user remembers the promise from the video and holds the app to it.

channels.name: moving from a tracker gone bad
channels.note: People in this niche live on one app for years until a redesign or a paywall shoves them out to look for a replacement. The leavers state precisely what they don't want, and that's a ready-made brief for a new tracker.

channels.name: wearables integration
channels.note: The watch itself suggests the brand: people learn about Natural Cycles because it's built into their smartwatch. A single signal, but the channel brings users without ads.

channels.name: store trawling and comparison
channels.note: Budgeters are methodical: they install several trackers in a row, test them, and keep one. The winner isn't the top search result, it's whoever survives the week of comparison. A full-featured free start is mandatory.

channels.name: moving from the desktop classics
channels.note: People migrate from Quicken and old YNAB to mobile equivalents. Whoever can take in their years of history gets a paying user ready-made.

channels.name: word of mouth: family and friends
channels.note: Budgets are often run as a couple, and one partner brings the other. Shared access works as a built-in growth mechanism.

channels.name: therapist's orders
channels.note: Therapists recommend gamified trackers to patients with ADHD. A rare channel but a precise one: for people who struggle with self-control, the app comes prescribed by a specialist.

channels.name: content for TikTok and YouTube
channels.note: People install the editor not for photos as such but for their channel: thumbnails, avatars, text for videos. The demand is born on the platforms, and the app lives as a creator's utility tool.

channels.name: found it on TikTok
channels.note: Flashy editors advertise themselves: the result is visible in other people's videos, and viewers go hunting for the tool. The wow effect in the feed drives installs without any direct advertising.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: A narrow task like captioning a photo gets searched with a direct store query. An app named precisely for the task takes that traffic.

channels.name: Instagram and Facebook ads
channels.note: Plant identifiers live on social video ads: the clip promises free magic from a photo. Almost everyone arriving through this channel complains about the pricing bait and switch, so an honest offer here is a competitive edge in itself.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The queries are concrete: a watering schedule, diagnosing a disease from a photo. People come with a task, not for a brand, so the door is open for a new app.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: The biggest entrance: people look for somewhere to put hundreds of recipes from magazines, books, and bookmarks, or a way to plan a week of meals. The queries are mature and specific, and the winner is whoever solves the task without a subscription upfront.

channels.name: the task comes from TikTok, Instagram, and Pinterest
channels.note: Demand is born on social media: people save recipes on TikTok and Instagram, then look for somewhere to keep them. Social import is the number one reason to install and the number one reason to delete when it fails.

channels.name: food influencers and ads
channels.note: A recommendation from a chef-blogger brings a wave of installs. Both paid integrations and a recipe author's own audience work, when the creator launches an app around their content.

channels.name: hopping between recipe managers
channels.note: Loyalty is low: users run two or three managers side by side, compare, and migrate chasing a specific import feature. Reviews name the competitors they left and the ones they left for.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends
channels.note: Ride-hailing spreads through friends, often literally: a friend orders the car from their own account, then the passenger installs the app themselves. Easy signup and a fast first pickup decide whether the newcomer stays.

channels.name: referral links and promo codes
channels.note: The niche classic: a discount for an invite. In reviews the channel shows up at the moment it breaks, a failed code turns a referred user into an unhappy one from day one.

channels.name: work requirement
channels.note: Driver apps aren't a choice, the job demands them. The audience is captive, but any glitch hits their income and lands in the reviews instantly.

channels.name: Instagram and Facebook ads
channels.note: Product videos and retargeting in the feed convert straight into installs. The user expects to find that exact item from the ad inside the app, and a break in that chain angers them immediately.

channels.name: word of mouth: family, friends, coworkers
channels.note: A great purchase and money saved make a story people retell to those close to them, a ready-made recommendation. Word-of-mouth arrivals come in warmer and forgive more.

channels.name: app-only discount
channels.note: The retailer herds people into installing with a promo code that only works in the app. The channel produces installs under duress, and a broken promo turns them into furious reviews.

channels.name: college recommendation
channels.note: A student discount service gets recommended by the colleges themselves. An institutional endorsement kills the scam fear from the first touch.

channels.name: social media and YouTube ads
channels.note: People with bad sleep click sleep ads on Facebook and YouTube themselves, but half the reviews from this channel are angry: the ad said free, then money got charged. The channel works when the promise in the video matches what's inside.

channels.name: the medical loop: CPAP, insurance, and doctors
channels.note: Some installs aren't the user's choice at all: the app ships with a CPAP machine, the insurer demands usage data, therapy platforms hand out discounts. For a new app this hints at partnerships with clinics and hardware makers.

channels.name: word of mouth: family, friends, and new moms
channels.note: People recommend it at the exact moment of need: a friend praises the tracker, a dad suggests white noise for a trip, a new mom gets the app right after the maternity ward. Moms then become ambassadors themselves and recommend it to every new mom they know.

channels.name: store search to replace a device or YouTube
channels.note: The app gets installed when the usual crutch breaks: the physical sound machine died, the ten-hour white noise videos on YouTube got old, the dog wakes everyone up at night. The demand is already hot, and the winner is whoever shows up for that specific task in store search.

channels.name: store search for a specific trip
channels.note: The install happens once the trip is on the calendar: someone searches for a Disneyland countdown, an RV route planner, or an expense tracker. The queries are razor-thin, and the winner is the app named and described in the language of the task.

channels.name: the travel agent puts the client on the app
channels.note: Some users never chose the app at all: the travel agent set it up, and the client is stuck living in it even when they want to edit the trip themselves. For a new product it's a ready-made B2B2C channel: sell to the agents and they bring the users.

channels.name: reddit as the pre-payment check
channels.note: Before booking and paying, people go read Reddit, and that's also where they find warnings about sketchy services. In a niche with hundreds of dollars on the line, forum reputation decides more than ads.

channels.name: recommendations: acquaintances and social media
channels.note: Isolated but lively signals: an entrepreneur friend praises the app, or it gets plugged hard on social media. People mass-harvest trip ideas from reels, so native posts in travel content land exactly at the planning moment.

channels.name: a show clip on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook
channels.note: The engine of every short-drama app: someone gets hooked on a clip in the feed, goes to the app to finish watching, and slams into a paywall. The channel is powerful but burns trust when the ad promises free and everything inside costs coins.

channels.name: an exclusive: a specific show, match, or streamer
channels.note: People subscribe not to the platform but to one thing: a series, the World Cup, a favorite streamer who only streams here. The install happens the moment the content drops, and without retention the subscription dies right after the finale.

channels.name: fleeing cable and free YouTube
channels.note: A noticeable share of the audience arrived while cutting the cord or trying to improve on free YouTube. They constantly compare price and ad load with the old option and drift back easily.

channels.name: a subscription bundled with another service
channels.note: A single but telling signal: the streaming came free with a grocery delivery subscription, and that's the only reason the person keeps it. Bundles with other subscriptions bring a passive audience that never would have installed on its own.

channels.name: moving on: Dark Sky died or the ads got unbearable
channels.note: The liveliest stream in the niche is refugees: some are still hunting for a replacement for the murdered Dark Sky, others ditch a familiar app once ads start covering the forecast. A new app just needs to be like the old one but without that, and say so in as many words.

channels.name: store search for a specific fear or task
channels.note: People don't install weather in general, they install a fix for an exact problem: reliable tornado alerts, storms along a trucker's route via CarPlay, a marine forecast for work. They choose by store description and rating, so a precise task statement in the listing decides.

channels.name: the local TV station calls from the broadcast
channels.note: Local stations' apps get installs straight from the air: anchors plug them on the news, and viewers follow the familiar meteorologist they've trusted for years. This channel is closed to an indie developer, but the template is free: people want a local voice, not a faceless forecast.

channels.name: word of mouth: family
channels.note: A rare but warm signal: the forecast gets shared inside the family as a trusted tool. Weather habits are inherited, the son showed it and the parent stayed.

channels.name: store search for your workout format
channels.note: People arrive with the query ready: free workouts, home training with no equipment, a beginner program, routines for seniors. They download the first thing matching the phrasing and get angry when a subscription hides behind free.

channels.name: doctor, physical therapist, and post-surgery recovery
channels.note: A noticeable stream of installs is prescribed by medicine: a physical therapist assigns an app with a home program, a doctor orders building muscle, surgery recovery calls for gentle workouts and progress tracking. The user is motivated and loyal but demands careful loads and an exact match to the prescription.

channels.name: Instagram and social media ads
channels.note: The niche classic: quiz funnels and bundles sell through aggressive retargeting, and it works, people download after the fifth impression. The flip side is classic too: the ad promises don't match the app, and the reviews overflow with the word scam.

channels.name: your own YouTube channel as a funnel
channels.note: HASfit spent years building an audience with free workouts on YouTube, and the trainers' fans came to the app to pay on their own. The channel is slow but delivers the warmest users, who forgive a lot as long as their favorite trainer is in the app.

channels.name: work and school demand PDF
channels.note: The main source of installs is obligation: work means scanning documents and receipts constantly, school and college mean submitting assignments as PDF. People install a scanner out of necessity, not love, so they tolerate a lot but quit at the first breakdown in their workflow.

channels.name: store search for a document needed right now
channels.note: The install happens at the moment of a burning task: fill out a form from the phone, scan a book, urgently turn a file into a PDF. People grab the first app promising free in the listing, and a lie on that word instantly turns into a furious review.

channels.name: Facebook ads
channels.note: Scanners buy Facebook ads, sometimes with wild promises up to scanning moles for cancer. The channel brings people, but the gap between the video and the app reads instantly and breeds distrust before the first scan.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends and coworkers
channels.note: The scanner gets recommended as a work tool, for example for tracking receipts in a business. A recommendation brings a loyal user, but the stakes rise too: a surprise paid export feels like betrayal.

channels.name: moving from Character.AI and ChatGPT
channels.note: The most powerful stream in the niche is refugees: Character.AI tightened limits and added a paywall, so people search for a c.ai alternative on purpose, while others got tired of ChatGPT or came from a dead service. A new app just needs to position itself as the alternative outright and not repeat the same limits.

channels.name: TikTok and social media ads
channels.note: Both flavors work: an organic TikTok recommendation brings roleplayers tired of limits, while paid ads promise avatars and features the app doesn't have and harvest angry reviews. One developer even asks users to make TikToks for rewards.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends
channels.note: Roleplay apps spread through friend circles: when the usual service goes bad, friends drag each other over to the replacement. A friend's recommendation instantly overrides distrust of an unknown brand.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: Some people aren't looking for AI in general but for a specific tool: a work assistant, an affordable image generator. They compare prices and capabilities and leave fast if the listing's promise doesn't match the product.

channels.name: store search: a simple timer without a subscription
channels.note: The dominant channel: people look for a fasting app on their own and repeat one request in almost every review, a simple timer without a subscription or extra bloat. The niche is overrun with paywalls, so an honest simple and free in the listing collects installs by itself.

channels.name: TikTok, Instagram, and Twitter ads
channels.note: Fasting app quiz funnels run in every feed and genuinely bring people in, but the ads systematically promise free while an expensive subscription waits inside, and reviews record it. An honest ad offer here is a competitive advantage all by itself.

channels.name: moving on after the death of Life app
channels.note: The shutdown of the popular tracker Life dumped seasoned loyal fasters onto the market, who cycled through replacements and even paid for duds. Dying competitors in this niche are a ready-made capture moment for a Life replacement page.

channels.name: a recommendation at the start of fasting
channels.note: A newcomer just starting intermittent fasting gets the app recommended along with the method itself, usually in communities and among friends. The moment of entering the practice is the point where a recommended tracker gets installed sight unseen.

channels.name: installing for a specific exam
channels.note: People come not for flashcards but for passing: USMLE, TOEFL, grad school admissions, a college course. A new app is better off targeting one exam with ready-made content than being an empty deck builder.

channels.name: tiktok and social media
channels.note: Students literally see the app in their feed and install it the same day. For the school and college audience, short videos showing a feature work as the main paid channel.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends and study groups
channels.note: Flashcards get studied in pairs and groups, so one happy user pulls in classmates or a Bible study circle. Shared decks and mutual accountability are baked into the scenario itself.

channels.name: a replacement for pricey anki
channels.note: Anki at $25 sends customers to its competitors all by itself: people want the same thing cheaper and want to import their decks. The working entrance to the niche is free spaced repetition plus honest import from Anki.

channels.name: a loved one speaks another language
channels.note: The liveliest install motive: a wife, a mom, or a friend speaks another language, and the translator becomes a bridge inside the family. These users test one specific language pair and leave forever if it's weak.

channels.name: a trip abroad
channels.note: The app gets installed right before vacation or already on the ground, and the buyer's main question is offline mode. Failing without internet in a foreign country means an instant refund and an angry review.

channels.name: store search with heavy comparison shopping
channels.note: People deliberately compare Google Translate alternatives: they read reviews and try several apps in a row against their own task. The rating and the first store screen genuinely sell here.

channels.name: ads on tiktok and in the feeds
channels.note: An ad with a slick translation demo works instantly, people install without a second thought. But it's also the top source of angry reviews when the promised language or feature doesn't work.

channels.name: word of mouth: runners pull in their own
channels.note: Running is social, a happy user literally migrates friends and family onto their app. A new product needs shared features and easy sharing, word of mouth is the main growth engine here.

channels.name: searching for a tracker for the task
channels.note: People search the store and google for a tracker for their exact case: free distance measuring, longboarding, even an electric scooter. A name and description tuned to a niche activity brings in the people Apple Fitness didn't fit.

channels.name: returning to a familiar program
channels.note: Runners quit and start over, and every spring they come back to the program that already worked once. Retention here isn't about streaks, it's about making the return after a break feel warm and shame-free.

channels.name: trainers' youtube content
channels.note: A single but telling signal: someone bought the app because they'd watched these trainers' channel for years. Expert content converts into installs without any advertising.

channels.name: school: lectures and assignments
channels.note: Students install a recorder for a specific class or assignment, often on deadline day. This audience has little money, and a hard paywall on the first recording draws the angriest reviews.

channels.name: work: meetings and clients
channels.note: Adults arrive with a work scenario: meeting minutes, long calls, a teacher's recordings for class. They install right before the meeting, so the first launch has to work with zero learning curve.

channels.name: recording a call for a dispute or protection
channels.note: Call recording gets bought in a stressful situation: a restraining order, a call with a lawyer, a dispute with a school. The stakes are high, and a failure on an important call gets avenged with one-star reviews and refunds.

channels.name: the store page: the rating decides
channels.note: People pick a recorder fast, straight off the stars in search results. Even a middling 3.7 reads as fine, I'll take it, so the app listing is the entire storefront.

channels.name: a job posting about to close
channels.note: Resumes get built at the last minute, sometimes on the day applications close, and people are ready to pay on the spot. It's a one-session product: if the PDF doesn't export right now, the money and the trust are gone forever.

channels.name: a phone instead of a laptop
channels.note: A noticeable share of the audience looks for a resume app because they simply don't own a laptop. The whole cycle from filling it out to applying for the job has to close on the phone, that's the very reason for the install.

channels.name: word of mouth: building resumes for loved ones
channels.note: One skilled person builds resumes for themselves, their family, and friends, so one install serves several job seekers. Multiple separate resumes in one account isn't abuse, it's a growth channel.

channels.name: switching over price hikes
channels.note: The niche's main current flows toward you: the leaders raise prices every year, and small businesses openly write that they're leaving to find a replacement. A stable cheap plan is an acquisition channel in itself, and the moment to catch people is the next price hike.

channels.name: word of mouth among small businesses
channels.note: Contractors recommend the tool to each other and even to their own clients. Small business circles are tight, one happy tradesman brings his whole crew.

channels.name: store search for a work need
channels.note: A tradesman looks for a service for a specific work scenario, like texting an invoice to a client right from the job site. The winner is whoever closes the narrow field task, not the biggest brand.

channels.name: app advertising
channels.note: Ads bring people in, but the promises in the video have to match the product. The only explicit review about ads is disappointment over a feature that doesn't exist.

channels.name: the 12-step program and treatment
channels.note: A sponsor flat out orders you to install the app, and rehab centers and halfway houses provide the context where it becomes a daily tool. Compatibility with AA language and rituals matters more here than any marketing.

channels.name: a method book leads to the app
channels.note: People first read Allen Carr or This Naked Mind, then look for a companion app to the method. A ready-made methodology with an audience is an open door for a new product.

channels.name: word of mouth: the family finds it
channels.note: The app is often found not by the addicted person but by a husband, wife, or daughter. The install becomes an act of care, so a simple onboarding for someone in crisis is critical.

channels.name: store search for a free tracker
channels.note: In the moment of resolve, a person searches the store for a free sobriety counter and grabs the first result. A paywall right after they've typed in their personal story feels like betrayal and breeds angry reviews.

channels.name: an urgent task right here, right now
channels.note: The scanner gets installed at the moment there's no way around it: paying for parking in an unfamiliar city, making a code for a funeral fundraiser, submitting a school project. The user is single-use and impatient, any obstacle before the result means deletion.

channels.name: store search for a code format
channels.note: Part of the audience isn't looking for a scanner in general but for a specific format like pdf417 or barcodes, and takes the first search result. Honest support for rare formats is a cheap way to grab that traffic.

channels.name: ads promising free
channels.note: People arrive from Safari ads and the promise of free, then a subscription costing tens of dollars is waiting inside. The channel works, but it's exactly what generates the stream of scam reviews.

channels.name: moving from a dead or degraded editor
channels.note: The loudest signal in the niche. People lived in iThoughts, Inspiration, or Lucid for years, and when those shut down, lost support, or jacked up prices, they went looking for a replacement. A new app should hunt these refugees head-on: a moving from iThoughts page and import of competitors' formats solve half of acquisition.

channels.name: school: students install it for note-taking
channels.note: Students in medicine, law, and STEM come on their own because linear notes stop working on complex subjects. They call the install a deliberate decision for their studies and are ready to pay. For a new app it's a ready-made segment: note templates and big maps with hundreds of nodes.

channels.name: store search for an exact task
channels.note: Some users arrive with a very specific ask: a map without a subscription, connections beyond parent-child, the best mapper period. They cycle through several apps and stay where the ask is covered. So precise store positioning around a feature beats a generic mind maps pitch.

channels.name: YouTube and video reviews
channels.note: Isolated but direct mentions: people come after YouTube videos, including ones by niche bloggers. A cheap channel for a launch, a review from a couple of productivity youtubers brings users already warmed up.

channels.name: TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram ads
channels.note: The niche's main pump. People install the app after a video with a spectacular live wallpaper, some get chased by the ad for weeks. But most of these reviews end angry: the promised wallpaper isn't inside or it's behind a subscription. The channel works if the advertised scene actually sits in the app for free, and that alone can set you apart from the whole niche.

channels.name: store search and trying lookalikes
channels.note: The second biggest road in: someone searches for wallpapers or widgets on a specific theme, downloads five similar apps in a day, and stays where they found what they wanted and the ads don't choke them. Marketing doesn't win here, precise coverage of the query and bearable first-minutes monetization does.

channels.name: word of mouth: family and friends
channels.note: A single but characteristic signal: customization gets shown by someone close right when a new phone is bought. It's a hint about the install moment, not about a channel at scale.

channels.name: youtube customization tutorials
channels.note: How to make your iphone aesthetic videos bring people in and train them at the same time, the user arrives with instructions in hand. One explicit mention, but for a launch it's a cheap channel: landing in a couple of tutorials is enough.

channels.name: store search: free water tracker
channels.note: Almost every explicit install story starts with a store search, and the key word in the query is free. Then specific wishes take over: Apple Watch sync, reminder intervals, a MyFitnessPal connection. People try several trackers back to back and rage at free for 3 days, so an honest free tier is a channel in itself.

channels.name: a medical reason: a diagnosis or the doctor's words
channels.note: The install happens after a jolt: a kidney diagnosis or a doctor's talk about water. That user is motivated and stays for the long haul. For a new app it's a hint toward onboarding for medical scenarios and clinic partnerships, though explicit mentions in reviews are few.

channels.name: specialists recommend it to clients
channels.note: Massage therapists, trainers, and other wellness pros recommend the tracker to clients as a working tool. A single signal, but it's a ready-made distribution mechanic: give the specialist a reason to recommend you while competitors scare their clients off with ads.

channels.name: a whole class or team at once
channels.note: One teacher's review shows the viral loop: the app lived with 600 students until ads killed it. Group scenarios (a class, a team, an office challenge) bring users in batches, and they leave in batches too.

channels.name: search and app-hopping for a specific task
channels.note: Owners come with a very concrete pain: monitoring barking while home alone, GPS instead of an AirTag, an all-in-one for pet health. They cycle through several apps and gadgets, read what gets recommended most, and stay where the task is covered. A new product needs to position itself around the task, not as a pet app.

channels.name: the vet clinic hands out the app
channels.note: A huge chunk of the niche runs on B2B2C: the clinic signs up for PetDesk, myVCA, or Thrive, and the owner installs the app because the vet said so. The user here is captive to the clinic's choice, but a good app genuinely keeps clients loyal to the clinic itself. For a founder it's a channel through vet partnerships, not the store.

channels.name: the emergency night: the pet is sick right now
channels.note: Televet apps get installed in a moment of panic, when the dog is sick at night and the clinic is out of reach. The user arrives cold and judges instantly by the first consultation. The channel is search results for vet 24/7, and the cost of a mistake in that moment is maximal.

channels.name: bundles with other subscriptions
channels.note: People learn about the service from Walmart+ or Healthy Paws insurance, where it comes as an add-on. The channel delivers distribution without marketing but brings users with someone else's expectations, which they then hold the service to.

channels.name: escaping a competitor that betrayed them
channels.note: The main inflow in this niche is refugees: 1Password moved everyone to subscriptions, Strongbox sold out, old managers died without updates for the new iOS. People leave angry and desperately looking for an alternative. A new product needs import from competitors' formats and a direct promise not to repeat the betrayal: one-time purchase, open format, export.

channels.name: a long store search on your own terms
channels.note: Some people spend years hunting for a manager that fits their personal requirements: no subscription, a plain list without autofill, or the exact opposite, an all-in-one. They compare several known products and pick by fit, not by brand. A precise store description of what this app is and who it's for converts exactly these people.

channels.name: word of mouth: a friend showed theirs
channels.note: Passwords are a sensitive topic, and a friend's recommendation removes the fear of trusting an unknown app. The signals are few but they run both ways: people get the tip from friends and also show their own manager to others.

channels.name: ideology and brand trust
channels.note: A single but telling motive: someone picks a less convenient product because of the company's privacy mission. In a niche where the product is trust, a public stance and reputation replace a marketing budget.

channels.name: feed ads with a viral template
channels.note: The niche is pumped by Instagram, Facebook, and Snapchat ads built around one specific scene: a dance with a baby, a birthday photo, a video with two dogs. People install the app for that one template. And in almost every such review the template turns out not to be inside, which ends in refunds and one-star ratings. The channel is powerful but only works if the advertised scene is one tap away after install.

channels.name: churning through generators until one works
channels.note: Experienced users run dozens of generators through their hands and settle where their personal criterion is met: no credits, stable quality, the right style. These people are more loyal than ad arrivals, and what brings them isn't marketing but a difference from the pack that shows in the first minutes.

channels.name: hunting for a replacement for Sora, Grok, Remini
channels.note: People look for alternatives to the big names: Sora shut down, everything useful in Grok is paid, Remini didn't cut it. They arrive expecting like that one but better and compare head to head. An alternative to X store positioning catches this traffic almost for free.

channels.name: word of mouth and other people's art on social media
channels.note: Some come through friends or after seeing the generations themselves: users' work on Twitter and YouTube serves as living advertising. So built-in sharing with an unobtrusive app credit is an acquisition channel, not just a feature.

channels.name: trying trackers until the best one
channels.note: The most common scenario: someone honestly tried nearly every tracker in the store and settled where the tracking was more accurate and daily entry simpler. Ads barely register here, the product wins. For a new app this means niche users can always be intercepted: they keep migrating until they find accuracy.

channels.name: store search for the task: taxes, gig work, your own garage
channels.note: The install comes with a specific trigger: a delivery driver needs mileage for taxes, an owner of a couple of cars needs a service log. People literally write searched and found. The queries are concrete, so an exact hit of name and description on the task wins, including the gig driver segment.

channels.name: replacing an app that broke or got complicated
channels.note: Part of the inflow is refugees from the old logs: Gas Buddy cut features, the previous tracker wouldn't sync across devices. This user arrives with their data history in hand, so importing old records turns their move from a pain into an argument for you.

channels.name: youtube gadget reviews
channels.note: A single signal but with a mechanic: the app comes bundled with an OBD device the person saw in a YouTube video. For hardware-plus-app combos, reviewers remain a working entry channel.

channels.name: store search: digitize the closet
channels.note: The most common entrance: someone has matured into the task on their own, a clothing catalog, outfit building, personal colors, and searches deliberately, some try several lookalikes, one even asked an AI for a list of apps. The key query words are free and builds outfits for me. A precise store description and a generous free start win.

channels.name: TikTok: videos and the ads dressed as them
channels.note: TikTok delivers volume but toxically: half the arrivals discover the video was an ad and what it showed is locked behind a subscription. The TikTok user is impulsive and writes the angry review instantly. The channel works when the video honestly equals free first value.

channels.name: fashion bloggers and press articles
channels.note: Fashion youtubers preaching wear your closet instead of buying new, plus press articles, bring a conscious audience. These users arrive with values and grill the product for living up to them, a blogger partnership obliges the product to hold the stated position.

channels.name: word of mouth: girlfriends and sisters
channels.note: Clothes are a social topic, outfits get discussed with people close to you, and the app gets passed along hand to hand. There's one explicit signal, but it shows the power of expectations: a friend raved about it, and a paid first step killed the interest on the spot.

channels.name: the shared list pulls in the other half
channels.note: The main reason to install isn't recipes, it's a shared list with a husband or wife. The second person in the couple gets the app by invitation from the first, so every family turns into two installs without any marketing.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: People come to the store with the phrasing ready: a simple weekly menu planner, a list sorted by store aisle. The winner is the app whose title and screenshots hit the query dead on.

channels.name: moving from a broken list
channels.note: A shopping list lives for years, people only leave when the old app breaks sync or loses data. On the way out they immediately look for a replacement, and that's a ready-made inbound stream for a new player.

channels.name: an ai assistant's tip
channels.note: A new entrance: someone describes the task to ChatGPT and installs whatever it named. Just one signal so far, but no competitor owns this channel, and it goes to whoever the models know about.

channels.name: coming back with the next pregnancy
channels.note: The tracker gets installed fresh for every pregnancy, and people pick the one they remember from last time. The market restarts every couple of years, so winning the first pregnancy brings the second and the third, and a spoiled impression loses them forever.

channels.name: word of mouth: girlfriends and family
channels.note: Pregnancy gets discussed with friends and sisters who've been through it, and the advice arrives together with an app name. It works for men too: dad guides get passed between future fathers.

channels.name: doctor's or insurer's orders
channels.note: The OB recommends a kick counter, the clinic or insurer hands out its own app for the benefits. The channel brings highly motivated users, but a mandated assignment doesn't forgive bugs: the person didn't come by choice.

channels.name: downloading mid-labor
channels.note: Contraction timers get installed at the last moment, sometimes literally in the delivery room. The decision takes seconds and rides on store search results, and a paywall or ads in that moment kill both the install and the rating.

channels.name: doctor's orders or a diagnosis
channels.note: The classic entrance to the niche: the doctor ordered a blood pressure log, there was a surgery or a diagnosis. Some doctors name the app themselves and then recommend it to other patients, a ready-made distribution loop for an honest log with export.

channels.name: ads promising to measure with the camera
channels.note: A huge stream of installs comes from TikTok and Instagram ads promising to measure blood pressure and sugar with a finger on the camera. People arrive, feel cheated, and torch the rating with one stars. The channel delivers volume but poisons trust in the whole niche.

channels.name: app store search for the job
channels.note: After buying a monitor or getting the doctor's orders, people go to the store for a simple log with a chart and a report. They try several in a row, and the winner gets decided in the first minutes: entry speed and clear export.

channels.name: the app bundled with the monitor
channels.note: Omron, Withings, iHealth, and A&D get installed because you bought the cuff, there's no choice involved. For an independent log it's both a competitor and an opening: the bundled apps annoy people regularly, and they look for somewhere to take their data.

channels.name: a challenge with family and friends
channels.note: The step counter gets installed to compete with a husband, relatives, and coworkers, and the install arrives as an invitation from someone already playing. The competitive mechanic recruits the next user by itself, right down to friends' referral codes.

channels.name: ads promising money for steps
channels.note: A noticeable part of the niche grows on get paid to install and walk ads. The promised money never gets paid out, and cheated users bury the reviews in the word scam. The channel delivers volume but an audience that leaves at the first failed cashout.

channels.name: store search for one specific little thing
channels.note: People don't install a step counter in general, they plug a hole: a steps widget for the home screen, monthly flights climbed, steps together with the route. A narrow feature put right in the title and screenshots catches this traffic.

channels.name: moving from a platform or a dead tracker
channels.note: Switching from Android to iPhone, plus buried apps like Moves, bought and shut down by Facebook, dump people with a formed habit onto the market. They search for same as what I had, and whoever promises exactly that takes them.

channels.name: exam around the corner: a targeted search
channels.note: The install is tied to the exam date: people search the store and the web one or two weeks before the test or right after failing it. Motivation peaks, and willingness to pay shows up exactly when the DMV is days away.

channels.name: word of mouth: friends, brothers, and sisters
channels.note: Licenses come in waves: classmates first, then younger brothers and sisters. Whoever passes hands the app to the next in line, and I passed with this one beats any ad.

channels.name: parents install and pay
channels.note: For teenagers the parent makes the call: registers, pays for the course, watches progress, and writes the reviews. The buyer and the user are different people, and the landing page and pricing need to talk to the parent.

channels.name: the job requires a cdl
channels.note: The adult segment comes for commercial licenses and endorsements: the CDL school hands out the textbook, and the person picks the app as a practice tool on their own. They come back when renewing endorsements, so the customer's life is longer than one exam.

channels.name: store search for a specific feature
channels.note: People search not for a weight tracker in general but for the missing piece: progress photos from three angles, weight together with calories, a decent chart. The install goes to the app whose store title and screenshots match that query exactly.

channels.name: in pairs for accountability
channels.note: People lose weight in pairs and teams: with a brother, a coworker, a wife. One person picks the app and pulls the rest in for the shared challenge, so team features turn every user into an acquisition channel.

channels.name: coming back for a new weight-loss attempt
channels.note: Weight loss is cyclical: on a new attempt people reinstall the tracker they remember from last time. The return often crashes into features that moved behind a subscription, and that's the moment a competitor's old users are up for grabs.

channels.name: instagram ads
channels.note: Diet trackers buy installs on social media, but both signals in reviews are about deception: they promised one thing, delivered another, and free turned into a charge. The channel exists, trust in it in this niche does not.

channels.name: bloggers and ads: youtube, tiktok, tv
channels.note: Brokers flood YouTube and television with ads featuring bonus rates and famous faces, finfluencers hand out promo codes, teenagers learn about the apps from TikTok. People come for the promised rate or a blogger's tip and get angry when the rate melts once they're in.

channels.name: a bonus for a friend: referrals
channels.note: The niche is trained to pay for referrals: deposit bonuses and invite-a-friend buttons are built in almost everywhere, and users genuinely come for them. But the bonus has to actually pay out, someone cheated on a referral takes revenge in the reviews.

channels.name: the employer: 401k and company stock
channels.note: A broker's app often isn't a choice: the employer keeps the retirement plan there or grants employees stock. The audience is captive and picky, and for a third-party product the way in is the job of pulling all accounts into one place.

channels.name: word of mouth in the family
channels.note: The investing family member pulls in the relatives: opens custodial accounts for the kids, an adult daughter signs up after her parent. A product that makes a first account for your own people easy gets these installs without marketing.
